newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices fall as Iraqi crude flows again.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fall as Iraqi crude flows again.

text.p: World crude oil prices fell on Tuesday after a report that Iraq had resumed crude oil exports for the first time since a 1990 U.N. embargo.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea for January delivery closed a sharp 81 cents lower at $23.25 a barrel after Iraqi media reported that President Saddam Hussein had pressed the button to restart flows of Iraqi oil.
But Iraqi celebrations later proved to be premature as technical problems prevented the first oil flow to Turkey's Ceyhan oil terminal.

It was not so much Iraq's much-delayed return to the oil market in the form of a partial oil export deal with the United Nations but the release of European Union stock data which pushed prices lower in the afternoon, traders said.

January Brent fell below a key support level at $23.77 a barrel after the data showed a heavy build in stocks of middle distillates, which include heating oil and have been a main market prop in a winter market hitherto low on stocks.
"We broke through key support and then just saw a continuation down," said one broker.
The absence of Iraqi crude from the oil markets was partly the reason why prices shot to a near six-year high in October when the U.N. oil-for-food deal was postponed from September.
Crude oil prices remain on average around $3.0 a barrel higher than this time last year.
Under the U.N. deal signed in May, Iraq will be allowed to sell $2.0 billion worth of crude oil for six months to buy food and medicines under strict U.N. supervision.

Iraq said it would pump 650,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil through its pipeline to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in Turkey and through its Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr under the U.N. plan cleared on Monday.
The Iraqi media reported celebrations in the northern Iraqi oil centre of Kirkuk after Iraqi President Saddam Hussein pushed the button to start the first exports.
But a Turkish oil official said later that no Iraqi oil had arrived at the terminal although he could not say if this was because of a reported fault at the Kirkuk pumping station.
Other than Turkey, no firm buyers have emerged from among the more than 50 oil company executives Iraq said had flocked to Baghdad to conclude term deals.
Turkey's state-owned refiner Tupras said it had signed a contract with Iraq's state oil marketing firm SOMO to buy 75,000 bpd of Iraqi oil under an agreement taking effect Tuesday.
Exports to the Far East were not expected before January, industry sources in Singapore said.

Iraq, before the Gulf War the second biggest oil producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) after Saudi Arabia, produced 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude in July 1990.
